A HYBRID REGISTRATION AND FUSION METHOD FOR HYPERSPECTRAL SUPER-RESOLUTION

Kunjing Yang
School of Mathematics
Hunan University
Changsha, Hunan 410082, P. R. China
kunjing-yang@hnu.edu.cn

Minru Bai
School of Mathematics
Hunan University
Changsha, Hunan 410082, P. R. China
minru-bai@hnu.edu.cn

Ting Lu
College of Electrical and Information Engineering
Hunan University
Changsha, Hunan 410082, P. R. China
tingluhnu@gmail.com

July 9, 2024

ABSTRACT

Fusing hyperspectral images (HSIs) with multispectral images (MSIs) has become a mainstream approach to enhance the spatial resolution of HSIs. Many HSI-MSI fusion methods have achieved impressive results. Nevertheless, certain challenges persist, including: (a) A majority of current methods rely on accurate registration of HSI and MSI, which can be challenging in real-world applications. (b) The obtained HSI-MSI pairs may not be fully utilized. In this paper, we propose a hybrid registration and fusion constrained optimization model named RAF-NLRGS. With respect to challenge (a), the RAF model integrates batch image alignment within the fusion process, facilitating simultaneous execution of image registration and fusion. To address issue (b), the NLRGS model incorporates a nonconvex low-rank and group-sparse structure, leveraging group sparsity to effectively harness valuable information embedded in the residual data. Moreover, the NLRGS model can further enhance fusion performance based on the RAF model. Subsequently, the RAF-NLRGS model is solved within the framework of Generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) algorithm and Proximal Alternating Optimization (PAO) algorithm. Theoretically, we establish the error bounds for the NLRGS model and the convergence analysis of corresponding algorithms is also presented. Finally, extensive numerical experiments on HSI datasets are conducted to verify the effectiveness of our method.

1 Introduction

Regular color images are limited to carrying information through three channels – red, green, and blue, whereas HSIs can encompass dozens or hundreds of continuous spectral bands. This enables HSIs to capture a wider range of the electromagnetic spectrum and provide more detailed spectral information. Considering various objects typically exhibit distinct reflectance characteristics, HSIs enable accurate recognition of materials, which is beneficial for many tasks, including anomaly detection [1] and disease monitoring [2].

However, the spatial resolution of HSIs frequently suffers from various factors, including sensor noise and constraints inherent to transmission systems [3]. Additionally, there exist fundamental physical limitations that lead to an inevitable trade-off between the spatial and spectral resolutions in HSIs, which limits their further practical applications [4]. In contrast, MSIs usually boast superior spatial resolution but compromises on spectral resolution. A feasible approach is to fuse the high spatial resolution MSI with a high spectral resolution HSI. In real-world applications, image registration serves as a crucial preprocessing step of fusion. Image registration involves meticulously aligning images through the application of spatial transformations to eradicate geometric discrepancies and ensure correspondence within a common coordinate system. A multitude of fusion methodologies overlook this crucial step, proceeding under the assumption that the images are perfectly aligned. Nevertheless, this assumption is difficult to realize since the registration of HSIs and MSIs presents a formidable challenge, largely due to their pronounced disparities in spatial resolution and spectral resolution [5]. To address the complexities of image registration task, certain researchers endeavor to execute registration and fusion processes concurrently. For example, Chen et al. [6] proposed leveraging a dynamic gradient sparsity property in the process of registering two images within the pansharpening task. Nevertheless, this approach does not fully exploit the intrinsic properties of the image. Unni et al. [7] developed a Plug and Play framework for HSI-MSI fusion tasks, which leverages neural networks to learn image priors and address the registration challenges. However, solving the subproblems requires pre-trained denoisers and registration networks, which entails a relatively high cost. The work in [8] presented an effective approach for simultaneous HSI super-resolution and geometric alignment of the image pair, incorporating spectral dictionary learning and sparse coding methods. Nonetheless, relying solely on sparse representation might not adequately capture the intrinsic features of the data.

To tackle these issues, we develop a constraint optimization model named RAF that simultaneously performs registration and fusion. This framework accounts for disparities across various bands within the HSI, incorporating batch image alignment into the fusion task, which applies distinct transformations to each band. Firstly, the RAF model capitalizes on the inherent spectral correlations within the HSI to project the target HSI onto a reduced-dimensional subspace, effectively diminishing the model’s dimensionality. Secondly, we employ a low-rank approximation approach to further explore the spatial correlations within the data. Thirdly, in recognition of the differences inherent among multi-source images due to variables like illumination changes and varying weather conditions, RAF model incorporates a linear transformation in the spectral domain of the MSI to reconcile and mitigate those discrepancies. Considering the inherent nonlinearity of the registration problem, we employ the Generalized Gauss–Newton (GGN) algorithm, which tackles it iteratively via a process of local linear approximations. Finally, convergence analysis of corresponding algorithms is also provided.

Considering the RAF model undertakes both registration and fusion tasks simultaneously, it may not consistently yield the most optimal fusion outcomes. Therefore, building upon the foundation of RAF model, we propose a novel NLRGS framework, which is specifically designed to optimize and bolster the performance of the fusion process. The RAF model furnishes NLRGS framework with registered HSI-MSI pairs and an advantageous initial point. This strategic integration has led to our two-stage method: RAF-NLRGS. For the fusion task, most methods concentrated on the reconstruction of primary information content, while neglecting the potential extraction of details from the residuals. Xu et al. [9] proposed an iterative regularization method that incorporates the residual into the original model for repeated calculation. While this methodology results in considerable enhancement, it is important to acknowledge that the residual information might not necessarily conform to the priors inherent in the original model, which may lead to a marked deceleration in computational efficiency during subsequent processing stages. Drawing inspiration from these insights, our NLRGS model, while integrating nonconvex low-rank techniques to reconstruct the primary part of the image, also employs a group sparsity prior to meticulously extract significant fine details from the residual data, which realizes a further enhancement in image quality. Then, Proximal Alternating Optimization (PAO) algorithm is applied to solve the NLRGS model. Theoretically, we establish error bounds for the NLRGS model and conduct convergence analysis of the PAO algorithm.

The main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • • We integrate batch image alignment into the HSI-MSI fusion problem and devise a constrained optimization model termed RAF. The RAF model is designed to concurrently execute both image registration and fusion tasks, while also adeptly managing spectral discrepancies across images originating from diverse sources.
  • • To further enhance fusion performance, we propose the NLRGS model, which features a nonconvex low-rank plus group sparse structure, enabling efficient recovery of both principal and detailed information. Simultaneously, we establish error bounds for the NLRGS model.
  • • The GGN and PAO algorithms are utilized to tackle the RAF and NLRGS models, respectively. Moreover, we provide a detailed convergence analysis of corresponding algorithms. Finally, extensive numerical experiments conducted on both simulated and real-world HSI datasets substantiate the efficacy of our proposed method.

Nonetheless, relying solely on sparse representation might not adequately capture the intrinsic features of the data.

This framework accounts for disparities across various bands within the HSI, incorporating batch image alignment into the fusion task, which applies distinct transformations to each band. Firstly, the RAF model capitalizes on the inherent spectral correlations within the HSI to project the target HSI onto a reduced-dimensional subspace, effectively diminishing the model's dimensionality. Secondly, we employ a low-rank approximation approach to further explore the spatial correlations within the data. Thirdly, in recognition of the differences inherent among multi-source images due to variables like illumination changes and varying weather conditions, RAF model incorporates a linear transformation in the spectral domain of the MSI to reconcile and mitigate those discrepancies. Considering the inherent nonlinearity of the registration problem, we employ the Generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) algorithm, which tackles it iteratively via a process of local linear approximations. Finally, convergence analysis of corresponding algorithms is also provided.

In real-world applications, image registration serves as a crucial preprocessing step of fusion. Image registration involves meticulously aligning images through the application of spatial transformations to eradicate geometric discrepancies and ensure correspondence within a common coordinate system. A multitude of fusion methodologies overlook this crucial step, proceeding under the assumption that the images are perfectly aligned. Nevertheless, this assumption is difficult to realize since the registration of HSIs and MSIs presents a formidable challenge, largely due to their pronounced disparities in spatial resolution and spectral resolution [5]. To address the complexities of image registration task, certain researchers endeavor to execute registration and fusion processes concurrently. For example, Chen *et al.* [6] proposed leveraging a dynamic gradient sparsity property in the process of registering two images within the pansharpening task. Nevertheless, this approach does not fully exploit the intrinsic properties of the image. Unni *et al.* [7] developed a Plug and Play framework for HSI-MSI fusion tasks, which leverages neural networks to learn image priors and address the registration challenges. However, solving the subproblems requires pre-trained denoisers and registration networks, which entails a relatively high cost. The work in [8] presented an effective approach for simultaneous HSI super-resolution and geometric alignment of the image pair, incorporating spectral dictionary learning and sparse coding methods. Nonetheless, relying solely on sparse representation might not adequately capture the intrinsic features of the data.

To tackle these issues, we develop a constraint optimization model named RAF that simultaneously performs registration and fusion. This framework accounts for disparities across various bands within the HSI, incorporating batch image alignment into the fusion task, which applies distinct transformations to each band. Firstly, the RAF model capitalizes on the inherent spectral correlations within the HSI to project the target HSI onto a reduced-dimensional subspace, effectively diminishing the model’s dimensionality. Secondly, we employ a low-rank approximation approach to further explore the spatial correlations within the data. Thirdly, in recognition of the differences inherent among multi-source images due to variables like illumination changes and varying weather conditions, RAF model incorporates a linear transformation in the spectral domain of the MSI to reconcile and mitigate those discrepancies. Considering the inherent nonlinearity of the registration problem, we employ the Generalized Gauss–Newton (GGN) algorithm, which tackles it iteratively via a process of local linear approximations. Finally, convergence analysis of corresponding algorithms is also provided.

Considering the RAF model undertakes both registration and fusion tasks simultaneously, it may not consistently yield the most optimal fusion outcomes. Therefore, building upon the foundation of RAF model, we propose a novel NLRGS framework, which is specifically designed to optimize and bolster the performance of the fusion process. The RAF model furnishes NLRGS framework with registered HSI-MSI pairs and an advantageous initial point. This strategic integration has led to our two-stage method: RAF-NLRGS. For the fusion task, most methods concentrated on the reconstruction of primary information content, while neglecting the potential extraction of details from the residuals. Xu *et al.* [9] proposed an iterative regularization method that incorporates the residual into the original model for repeated calculation. While this methodology results in considerable enhancement, it is important to acknowledge that the residual information might not necessarily conform to the priors inherent in the original model, which may lead to a marked deceleration in computational efficiency during subsequent processing stages. Drawing inspiration from these insights, our NLRGS model, while integrating nonconvex low-rank techniques to reconstruct the principal part of the image, also employs a group sparsity prior to meticulously extract significant fine details from the residual data, realizes a further enhancement in image quality. Then, Proximal Alternating Optimization (PAO) algorithm is applied to solve the NLRGS model. Theoretically, we establish error bounds for the NLRGS model and conduct convergence analysis of the PAO algorithm.

The main contributions are summarized as follows:

• We integrate batch image alignment into the HSI-MSI fusion problem and devise a constrained optimization model termed RAF. The RAF model is designed to concurrently execute both image registration and fusion tasks, while also adeptly managing spectral discrepancies across images originating from diverse sources.

• To further enhance fusion performance, we propose the NLRGS model, which features a nonconvex low-rank plus group sparse structure, enabling efficient recovery of both principal and detailed information. Simultaneously, we establish error bounds for the NLRGS model.

• The GGN and PAO algorithms are utilized to tackle the RAF and NLRGS models, respectively. Moreover, we provide a detailed convergence analysis of corresponding algorithms. Finally, extensive numerical experiments conducted on both simulated and real-world HSI datasets substantiate the efficacy of our proposed method.

2 Related work

2.1 Image registration

Image registration serves as a pivotal preprocessing step in image fusion, which can fundamentally be divided into two primary categories: feature-based and intensity-based approaches. In the realm of feature-based algorithms, Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) [10] is a distinguished technique and has made significant strides in computer vision applications. To boost the computational efficiency of SIFT, Bay et al. [11] incorporated the Hessian matrix into the SIFT framework and developed the Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF) algorithm. The research in [12] involves extracting feature points using the Accelerated Segment Test (FAST) algorithm, significantly diminishing computational time requirements. Radiation variation Insensitive Feature Transform (RIFT) [13] capitalized on the phase congruency principle, known for its robustness against changes in lighting and radiometric variations, to formulate discriminative descriptors specifically tailored for multi-sensor image registration.

Intensity-based registration algorithms embrace a holistic pixel-wise approach, wherein they introduce quantitative measures that effectively embody the image’s consistency for purposes of image alignment, e.g., Mutual Information (MI) [14]. Myronenko et al. [15] proposed an alignment method that hinges on minimizing the Residual Complexity (RC) between two images, an indicator that quantifies the sparsity of the residual image ensuing from the alignment process. Chen et al. [16] introduced a novel measure termed Normalized Total Gradient, assuming that the gradient of the difference between a pair of well-aligned images exhibits a higher degree of sparsity. Li et al. [17] proposed a novel similarity measure based on the registered images can be sparsified hierarchically in the gradient domain and frequency domain with the separation of sparse errors. Cao et al. presented [18] a Structure Consistency Boosting (SCB) transformation, which is designed to enhance the structural resemblance between MSIs.

Beyond pairwise image registration, batch image alignment refers to the procedure of aligning a group of interconnected images. Peng et al. [19] utilized the sparse and low-rank decomposition and identify an optimal set of image domain transformations to align a batch of linearly correlated images. However, they vectorize each grayscale image, which destroys the inherent correlation. Zhang et al. [20] proposed a convex image alignment method from the perspective of tensors, and provided an analysis of the error bounds. Xia et al. [21] incorporated transformed tensor-tensor products and nonconvex l_p norm regularization for image alignment.

2.2 HSI-MSI fusion

Existing approaches for HSI-MSI fusion mainly encompass three categories: deep learning-based, matrix factorization (MF)-based and tensor factorization (TF)-based methods. Deep learning-based methods leverage neural networks to glean the inherent features between HSI and MSI data, then the networks synthesize a fused image that effectively integrates the spatial detail and spectral attributes from both datasets [22]. Dian et al. [23] enhanced the model’s adaptability by downsampling the images destined for fusion to create training data, which is subsequently employed to train the neural network. MF-based methods explore the internal correlations within images to reduce problem dimensions or perform component separation. Yokoya et al. [24] proposed a Coupled Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (CNMF) fusion technique rooted in the principles of a linear spectral mixture model, which decomposes the spectral information to effectively integrate and fuse data. Dong et al. [25] developed a Nonnegative Structured Sparse Representation (NSSR) method which jointly estimated the dictionary and the sparse coefficients. However, MF-based methods require the initial unfolding of three-dimensional data into matrices, a process that may inadvertently undermine the intrinsic structural integrity of the data and potentially lead to a reduction in the efficacy of image restoration or reconstruction.

Recently, TF-based methods have demonstrated a superior capacity for leveraging the multilinear features of the data in comparison to MF-based methods [26]. In [27], the target HSI was restructured as a CP approximation and an alternating least squares algorithm called Super-resolution TEnsor REconstruction (STEREO) was developed. Zeng et al. [28] utilized CP factorization to characterize the low-rank structure of HSIs with a sparse Bayesian framework for adaptive rank determination. Li et al. [29] proposed a methodology employing Coupled Sparse Tucker Factorization (CSTF) for HSI-MSI fusion. The work in [30] employed nonlocal clustering and low Tensor-Train rank representation (LTTR) as regularization to enhance the model’s performance and robustness. Chen et al. ### 2.1 Image registration

Image registration serves as a pivotal preprocessing step in image fusion, which can fundamentally be divided into two primary categories: feature-based and intensity-based approaches. In the realm of feature-based algorithms, Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) [10] is a distinguished technique and has made significant strides in computer vision applications. To boost the computational efficiency of SIFT, Bay _et al._ [11] incorporated the Hessian matrix into the SIFT framework and developed the Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF) algorithm. The research in [12] involves extracting feature points using the Accelerated Segment Test (FAST) algorithm, significantly diminishing computational time requirements. Radiation variation Insensitive Feature Transform (RIFT) [13] capitalized on the phase congruency principle, known for its robustness against changes in lighting and radiometric variations, to formulate discriminative descriptors specifically tailored for multi-sensor image registration.

Intensity-based registration algorithms embrace a holistic pixel-wise approach, wherein they introduce quantitative measures that effectively embody the image’s consistency for purposes of image alignment, e.g., Mutual Information (MI) [14]. Myronenko _et al._ [15] proposed an alignment method that hinges on minimizing the Residual Complexity (RC) between two images, an indicator that quantifies the sparsity of the residual image ensuing from the alignment process. Chen _et al._ [16] introduced a novel measure termed Normalized Total Gradient, assuming that the gradient of the difference between a pair of well-aligned images exhibits a higher degree of sparsity. Li _et al._ [17] proposed a novel similarity measure based on the registered images can be sparsified hierarchically in the gradient domain and frequency domain with the separation of sparse errors. Cao _et al._ presented [18] a Structure Consistency Boosting (SCB) transformation, which is designed to enhance the structural resemblance between MSIs.

Beyond pairwise image registration, batch image alignment refers to the procedure of aligning a group of interconnected images. Peng _et al._ [19] utilized the sparse and low-rank decomposition and identify an optimal set of image domain transformations to align a batch of linearly correlated images. However, they vectorize each grayscale image, which destroys the inherent correlation. Existing approaches for HSI-MSI fusion mainly encompass three categories: deep learning-based, matrix factorization (MF)-based and tensor factorization (TF)-based methods. Deep learning-based methods leverage neural networks to glean the inherent features between HSI and MSI data, then the networks synthesize a fused image that effectively integrates the spatial detail and spectral attributes from both datasets [22]. Dian et al. [23] enhanced the model’s adaptability by downsampling the images destined for fusion to create training data, which is subsequently employed to train the neural network. MF-based methods explore the internal correlations within images to reduce problem dimensions or perform component separation. Yokoya et al. [24] proposed a Coupled Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (CNMF) fusion technique rooted in the principles of a linear spectral mixture model, which decomposes the spectral information to effectively integrate and fuse data. Dong et al. [25] developed a Nonnegative Structured Sparse Representation (NSSR) method which jointly estimated the dictionary and the sparse coefficients. However, MF-based methods require the initial unfolding of three-dimensional data into matrices, a process that may inadvertently undermine the intrinsic structural integrity of the data and potentially lead to a reduction in the efficacy of image restoration or reconstruction.

Recently, TF-based methods have demonstrated a superior capacity for leveraging the multilinear features of the data in comparison to MF-based methods [26]. [31] developed a fusion method based on Tensor Ring (TR) decomposition and a factor smoothed regularization was used to encapsulate the

2.3 Registration-fusion method

In addition to the concurrent registration and fusion approaches mentioned in introduction, there are also research focusing on a two-stage methodology. This strategy revolves around a sequential framework that begins with the execution of image registration, followed by the subsequent undertaking of the fusion process. Zhou et al. [33] proposed a integrated registration and fusion method that minimized a least-squares objective function by utilizing the point spread function (PSF). Ying et al. [34] introduce a new registration method NED for clear-blur image similarity measurement and incorporate the interpolation process into the fusion process. Guo et al. [35] utilized prior geographical information for pre-registration using Rational Polynomial Coefficient (RPC) orthorectification, then a CNN-based network is proposed to optimize the image registration and blur kernel learning jointly, culminating in the execution of the fusion process.

3.1 Preliminary

In this paper, we consistently employ the following notation conventions: scalars are represented by lowercase letters, such as 'a'; vectors are denoted by bold lowercase letters such as 'a'; matrices are represented by bold uppercase letters such as 'A'; tensors are denoted by calligraphic letters such as 'A'; sets and fields are denoted by hollow letters such as 'R'. Both \|\cdot\|_F and \|\cdot\| represent the Frobenius norm. Next, we present a concise introduction of tensor algebra. Readers can refer to [36] for a more comprehensive exposition on tensor.

Definition 3.1. (F-diagonal Tensor [37]) A tensor \mathcal{X} is called f-diagonal if each frontal slice \mathcal{X}^{(i)} is a diagonal matrix.

Definition 3.2. (Tensor Singular Value Decomposition: t-SVD [37]) For \mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_1 \times n_2 \times n_3}, the t-SVD of \mathcal{X} is given by \mathcal{X} = \mathcal{U} * \mathcal{S} * \mathcal{V}^H, where \mathcal{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_1 \times n_1 \times n_3} and \mathcal{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_2 \times n_2 \times n_3} are orthogonal tensors, \mathcal{V}^H denotes the conjugate transpose of \mathcal{V} and \mathcal{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_1 \times n_2 \times n_3} is a f-diagonal tensor. The entries in \mathcal{S} are called the singular fibers of \mathcal{X} and * denotes the t-product.

Definition 3.3. (Tensor Average Rank [37]) For \mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_1 \times n_2 \times n_3}, the tensor average rank, denoted as rank_a(\mathcal{X}), is defined as rank_a(\mathcal{X}) = \frac{1}{n_3} \sum_{i=1}^{n_3} rank(\hat{\mathcal{X}}^{(i)}), where \hat{\mathcal{X}}^{(i)} is the i th frontal slice of \hat{\mathcal{X}}, and \hat{\mathcal{X}} := fft(\mathcal{X}, [ ], 3). Here fft represents the Fast Fourier Transform.

Definition 3.4. (Tensor Nuclear Norm [37]) The TNN of \mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_1 \times n_2 \times n_3} is the average of the nuclear norm of all the frontal slices of \hat{\mathcal{X}}, i.e., \|\mathcal{X}\|_{TNN} = \frac{1}{n_3} \sum_{i=1}^{n_3} \|\hat{\mathcal{X}}^{(i)}\|_*, where \|\cdot\|_* denotes the nuclear norm of a matrix.

In the following, a class of functions will be presented, accompanied by their respective proximal mappings. We initially make the following assumptions for the function \psi.

Assumption 3.1. (a). \psi : \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} is proper, lower semicontinuous and symmetric with respect to y-axis; (b). \psi is concave and monotonically nondecreasing on [0, +\infty) with \psi(0) = 0.

In fact, many commonly used functions in statistics satisfy Assumption 3.1. We list three of them as follows:

  • • l_1 [38]: \psi^{l_1}(x) = |x|;
  • • Logarithm [39]: \psi^{log}(x) = \log(|x| + \theta), \theta > 0;
  • • MCP [40]: \psi^{MCP}(x) = \begin{cases} |x| - \frac{x^2}{2\theta}, & |x| \leq \theta, \\ \frac{\theta^2}{2}, & |x| > \theta. \end{cases}

We now present the definition of the proximal mapping.

Definition 3.5. (Proximal Mapping) The proximal operator of z \in \mathbb{R} with respect to function \psi is defined as

\text{prox}_{\alpha\psi}(z) := \arg \min_x \left\{ \alpha\psi(x) + \frac{1}{2}(x - z)^2 \right\}.

The proximal mappings of above functions have closed-form solution, which can be found in the Appendix A.

3.2 Problem formulation

HSIs and MSIs can be considered as three-dimensional tensors. We represent the target high-resolution HSI (HR-HSI) as \mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N \times H}, where M and N denote the two spatial dimensions, and H represents the number of spectral bands. Similarly, the obtained HSIs and MSIs are denoted as \mathcal{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n \times H} and \mathcal{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N \times h} respectively, where m < M, n < N, and h < H.

The derived HSI \mathcal{Y} can be perceived as a spatially degraded variant of the target HR-HSI \mathcal{X}. Therefore, the relationship between \mathcal{X} and \mathcal{Y} can be expressed as

\mathcal{Y}_{(3)} = \mathcal{X}_{(3)} \mathbf{BS} + \mathbf{N}_1, \quad (1)

where the subscript (\cdot)_{(3)} denotes the mode-3 unfolding matrix of a tensor. \mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{MN \times MN} is a spatial blurring matrix representing the hyperspectral sensor's point spread function (PSF), which is assumed band-independent and operates under circular boundary conditions [41]. \mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{MN \times mn} is a downsampling matrix, whose column vectors form a subset of the identity matrix. Matrix \mathbf{N}_1 represents the noise, with the assumption that it follows the Gaussian distribution. Similarly, the acquired MSI \mathcal{Z} can be considered as the degraded version of HR-HSI \mathcal{X} along the spectral mode. Therefore, the relationship between \mathcal{X} and \mathcal{Z} can be expressed as follows:

\mathcal{Z}_{(3)} = \mathbf{R} \mathcal{X}_{(3)} + \mathbf{N}_2, \quad (2)

where \mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times H} is the spectral downsampling matrix, and \mathbf{N}_2 is the Gaussian noise contained in the observed MSI. For simplicity, we rewrite (1) and (2) as:

\mathcal{Y} = \mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{X}) + \mathcal{N}_1, \quad \mathcal{Z} = \mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{X}) + \mathcal{N}_2, \quad (3)

where \mathcal{H}_{spa} and \mathcal{H}_{spec} represent spatial and spectral degradation operators. Their specific expressions are as follows:

\begin{aligned} \mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{X}) &:= \text{fold}_3(\text{unfold}_3(\mathcal{X}) \cdot \mathbf{BS}), \\ \mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{X}) &:= \text{fold}_3(\mathbf{R} \cdot \text{unfold}_3(\mathcal{X})), \end{aligned}

where \text{unfold}_3(\cdot) represents the mode-3 unfolding matrix of a tensor and \text{fold}_3(\cdot) denotes its inverse operator.

Considering that there may be infinite solutions satisfying equation (3), it is necessary to investigate the prior characteristics of the images to narrow down the scope of the solution space and find solutions that better align with our expectations.

It is noteworthy that in practical scenarios, the HSI-MSI pairs acquired from different sensors may exhibit poor registration. Consequently, it is imperative to conduct image registration preprocessing prior to fusion. Considering the inherent discrepancies among different spectral bands within HSIs, we treat HSIs as a collection of individual grayscale images and apply spatial transformations to each spectral band of HSI to achieve piecewise registration with respect to the MSI. Specifically, we need to find a transformation \tau to ensure \mathcal{Y} \circ \tau is aligned with the MSI. Here \mathcal{Y} \circ \tau is defined as

(\mathcal{Y} \circ \tau)_i = \mathcal{Y}_i \circ \tau_i,

where \tau denotes the mapping that consists of H transformations \{\tau_i, i = 1, \dots, H\} and \mathcal{Y} \circ \tau represents image \mathcal{Y} warped by \tau. The (\cdot)_i represents corresponding ith band.

3.3 Some fundamental assumptions

With respect to the issues of image fusion and registration tasks, we make some fundamental assumptions to facilitate further theoretical analysis. For degradation operators \mathcal{H}_{spa} and \mathcal{H}_{spec}, we first introduce the restricted eigenvalue (RE) condition as follows.

Definition 3.6. The operator \mathcal{H} is said to satisfy the restricted eigenvalue condition relative to constant s (REC(s)) if

\xi(s) := \min_{\mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{X}_s} \frac{\|\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{X})\|_F}{\|\mathcal{X}\|_F} > 0,

where \mathbb{X}_s represents some set related to s > 0.

3.2 Problem formulation
HSIs and MSIs can be considered as three-dimensional tensors. We represent the target high-resolution HSI (HR-HSI) as 𝒳 ∈ ℝM×N×H, where M and N denote the two spatial dimensions, and H represents the number of spectral bands. Similarly, the obtained HSIs and MSIs are denoted as 𝒴 ∈ ℝm×n×H and 𝒵 ∈ ℝM×N×h respectively, where m < M, n < N, and h < H.
The derived HSI 𝒴 can be perceived as a spatially degraded variant of the target HR-HSI 𝒳. Therefore, the relationship between 𝒳 and 𝒴 can be expressed as
𝒴(3) = 𝒳(3)BS + N1,                                                                                                             (1)
where the subscript (·)(3) denotes the mode-3 unfolding matrix of a tensor. B ∈ ℝMN×MN is a spatial blurring matrix representing the hyperspectral sensor's point spread function(PSF), which is assumed band-independent and operates under circular boundary conditions [41]. S ∈ ℝMN×mn is a downsampling matrix, whose column vectors form a subset of the identity matrix. Matrix N1 represents the noise, with the assumption that it follows the Gaussian distribution. Similarly, the acquired MSI 𝒵 can be considered as the degraded version of HR-HSI 𝒳 along the spectral mode. Therefore, the relationship between 𝒳 and 𝒵 can be expressed as follows:
𝒵(3) = R𝒳(3) + N2,                                                                                                             (2)
where R ∈ ℝh×H is the spectral downsampling matrix, and N2 is the Gaussian noise contained in the observed MSI. For simplicity, we rewrite (1) and (2) as:
𝒴 = ℋspa(𝒳) + 𝒩1,     𝒵 = ℋspec(𝒳) + 𝒩2,                                                          (3)
where ℋspa and ℋspec represent spatial and spectral degradation operators. Their specific expressions are as follows:
ℋspa(𝒳) := fold3(unfold3(𝒳) · BS),
ℋspec(𝒳) := fold3(R · unfold3(𝒳)),
where unfold3(·) represents the mode-3 unfolding matrix of a tensor and fold3(·) denotes its inverse operator.
Considering that there may be infinite solutions satisfying equation (3), it is necessary to investigate the prior characteristics of the images to narrow down the scope of the solution space and find solutions that better align with our expectations.
It is noteworthy that in practical scenarios, the HSI-MSI pairs acquired from different sensors may exhibit poor registration. Consequently, it is imperative to conduct image registration preprocessing prior to fusion. Considering the inherent discrepancies among different spectral bands within HSIs, we treat HSIs as a collection of individual grayscale images and apply spatial transformations to each spectral band of HSI to achieve piecewise registration with respect to the MSI. Specifically, we need to find a transformation τ to ensure 𝒴 ∘ τ is aligned with the MSI. Here 𝒴 ∘ τ is defined as
(𝒴 ∘ τ)i = 𝒴i ∘ τi,
where τ denotes the mapping that consists of H transformations {τi, i = 1, ···, H} and 𝒴 ∘ τ represents image 𝒴 warped by τ. The (·)i represents corresponding ith band.

ξ(s) := min𝒳∈𝕏s ‖ℋ(𝒳)‖F/‖𝒳‖F > 0,

## 3.2 Problem formulation

HSIs and MSIs can be considered as three-dimensional tensors. We represent the target high-resolution HSI (HR-HSI) as \(\mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N \times H}\), where \(M\) and \(N\) denote the two spatial dimensions, and \(H\) represents the number of spectral bands. Similarly, the obtained HSIs and MSIs are denoted as \(\mathcal{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n \times H}\) and \(\mathcal{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N \times h}\) respectively, where \(m < M\), \(n < N\), and \(h < H\).

The derived HSI \(\mathcal{Y}\) can be perceived as a spatially degraded variant of the target HR-HSI \(\mathcal{X}\). Therefore, the relationship between \(\mathcal{X}\) and \(\mathcal{Y}\) can be expressed as

\[
\mathcal{Y}_{(3)} = \mathcal{X}_{(3)}\mathbf{BS} + \mathbf{N}_1,
\tag{1}
\]

where the subscript \((\cdot)_{(3)}\) denotes the mode-3 unfolding matrix of a tensor. \(\mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{MN \times MN}\) is a spatial blurring matrix representing the hyperspectral sensor’s point spread function(PSF), which is assumed band-independent and operates under circular boundary conditions [41]. \(\mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{MN \times mn}\) is a downsampling matrix, whose column vectors form a subset of the identity matrix. Matrix \(\mathbf{N}_1\) represents the noise, with the assumption that it follows the Gaussian distribution. Similarly, the acquired MSI \(\mathcal{Z}\) can be considered as the degraded version of HR-HSI \(\mathcal{X}\) along the spectral mode. Therefore, the relationship between \(\mathcal{X}\) and \(\mathcal{Z}\) can be expressed as follows:

\[
\mathcal{Z}_{(3)} = \mathbf{R}\mathcal{X}_{(3)} + \mathbf{N}_2,
\tag{2}
\]

\]

\[
\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{X}) := fold_3(unfold_3(\mathcal{X}) \cdot \mathbf{BS}),
\]

\[
\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{X}) := fold_3(\mathbf{R} \cdot unfold_3(\mathcal{X})),
\]

where \(unfold_3(\cdot)\) represents the mode-3 unfolding matrix of a tensor and \(fold_3(\cdot)\) denotes its inverse operator.

\[

\]

where \(\tau\) denotes the mapping that consists of \(H\) transformations \(\{\tau_i, i = 1, \cdots, H\}\) and \(\mathcal{Y} \circ \tau\) represents image \(\mathcal{Y}\) warped by \(\tau\). The \((\cdot)_i\) represents corresponding \(i\)th band.

4.1.1 The RAF model

Given that HSIs typically encompass numerous spectral bands with high spectral correlation, we leverage subspace representation for \mathcal{X}, i.e.,

\mathcal{X} = \mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}, \quad (4)

where \mathcal{L} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N \times L} is the coefficient tensor, \mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times L} denotes the dictionary and L represents the dimension of the subspace spanned by the columns of \mathbf{D}. To estimate dictionary \mathbf{D}, a commonly adopted assumption is that \mathcal{Y} and \mathcal{X} share a common spectral subspace. Employing this principle, we estimate the dictionary \mathbf{D} from the LR-HSI by applying truncated singular value decomposition (svd), i.e.,

[\mathbf{U}, \Sigma, \mathbf{V}] = \text{svd}(\mathbf{Y}_{(3)}) \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{D} = \mathbf{U}(:, 1 : L), \quad (5)

where \Sigma denotes the matrix whose diagonal elements are the singular values of \mathbf{Y}_{(3)}. \mathbf{U} and \mathbf{V} are the left and right singular matrices, respectively.

Equations (4) utilized the spectral correlation of HSI to reduce the dimensionality of the problem. Next, we explore the spatial correlation of coefficient tensor \mathcal{L} to further enhance the model's performance. Specifically, we adopt the tensor nuclear norm (TNN) to characterize the low-rankness of coefficient tensor.

Moreover, it is recognized that disparities in imaging satellites, illumination conditions, and acquisition times can engender significant spectral variations between images [35], i.e., \mathcal{Y} and \mathcal{Z} come from different HR-HSIs. Thus, we incorporate a linear transformation to the spectral dimension of \mathcal{Z}. Finally, the RAF model is developed as follows:

\begin{aligned} \min_{\mathcal{L}, \tau, \mathbf{A}, \mathcal{B}} \quad & \|\mathcal{L}\|_{\text{TNN}}, \\ \text{s.t.} \quad & \mathcal{H}_{\text{spa}}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) = \mathcal{Y} \circ \tau, \\ & \mathcal{H}_{\text{spec}}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) = \mathcal{Z} \times_3 \mathbf{A} + \mathcal{B}, \end{aligned} \quad (6)

where \mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times h} and \mathcal{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N \times h} are utilized to eradicate spectral discrepancies between images.

4.1.2 GGN algorithm for solving the RAF model

As a matter of fact, the equality constraint of (6) is highly nonlinear due to the domain transformations \tau, which complicates the minimization task. Therefore, we employ the Generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) algorithm, which involves leveraging a first-order approximation of \tau when the variations in \tau are relatively insignificant [19]. Specifically, under small perturbation \Delta\tau, we have \mathcal{Y} \circ (\tau + \Delta\tau) \approx \mathcal{Y} \circ \tau + \mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau), with \mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau) := \text{fold}_3((\sum_{i=1}^H \mathbf{J}_i \Delta\tau \epsilon_i \epsilon_i^\top)^\top), where \mathbf{J}_i = \frac{\partial}{\partial \xi} \text{vec}(\mathcal{Y}_i \circ \xi)|_{\xi=\tau_i} is the Jacobian matrix of the ith image with respect to the transformation parameters \tau_i and \{\epsilon_i\} denotes the standard basis for \mathbb{R}^H. After adopting a local first-order approximation for a given \tau^k, we obtain the following subproblem:

\begin{aligned} \min_{\mathcal{L}, \Delta\tau, \mathbf{A}, \mathcal{B}} \quad & \|\mathcal{L}\|_{\text{TNN}}, \\ \text{s.t.} \quad & \mathcal{H}_{\text{spa}}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) = \mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^k + \mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau), \\ & \mathcal{H}_{\text{spec}}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) = \mathcal{Z} \times_3 \mathbf{A} + \mathcal{B}. \end{aligned} \quad (7)

Considering that subproblem (7) constitutes a local linearization of RAF model at the point \tau^k, we proceed to treat \tau^k + \Delta\tau as the next iterative estimate and undertake another cycle of linearization. The entire procedure described above is summarized in Algorithm 1.

For the termination criterion of the algorithm, we define

\kappa_{\text{raf}} := \frac{\|\mathcal{H}_{\text{spec}}(\mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^{k+1}) - \mathcal{H}_{\text{spa}}(\mathcal{Z} \times_3 \mathbf{A}^{k+1} + \mathcal{B}^{k+1})\|}{\|\mathcal{H}_{\text{spa}}(\mathcal{Z})\|}.

The algorithm terminates when \kappa_{\text{raf}} falls below a predetermined threshold. Next, we delve into the convergence properties associated with Algorithm 1.

Theorem 4.1. Suppose the operator \mathcal{H}_{\text{spa}} satisfies \text{REC}(s) on set \mathbb{X}_s := \{\mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N \times H} \mid \text{rank}(\mathcal{X}_{(3)}) \leq s\}, where s denotes the dimension of the null space of \mathcal{H}_{\text{spa}}(\cdot), then Algorithm 1 converges quadratically in the neighborhood of any strongly unique local minimum of (6).

The proof is provided in the Appendix B.

Remark 4.1. Within the framework of the RAF model, the obtained \mathcal{X} can be decomposed into \mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}, which indicates that \text{rank}(\mathcal{X}_{(3)}) \leq \text{rank}(\mathcal{L}_{(3)}) \leq L. Consequently, L serves as an upper threshold on the value of s, inherently suggesting that s is constrained from becoming excessively large.

4.1.1 The RAF model

Given that HSIs typically encompass numerous spectral bands with high spectral correlation, we leverage subspace
representation for $\mathcal{X}$, i.e.,

$$
\mathcal{X} = \mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}, \tag{4}
$$

where $\mathcal{L} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N \times L}$ is the coefficient tensor, $\mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times L}$ denotes the dictionary and $L$ represents the dimension of the subspace spanned by the columns of $\mathbf{D}$. To estimate dictionary $\mathbf{D}$, a commonly adopted assumption is that $\mathcal{Y}$ and $\mathcal{X}$ share a common spectral subspace. Employing this principle, we estimate the dictionary $\mathbf{D}$ from the LR-HSI by applying truncated singular value decomposition (svd), i.e.,

$$
[\mathbf{U}, \mathbf{\Sigma}, \mathbf{V}] = \text{svd}(\mathbf{Y}_{(3)}) \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{D} = \mathbf{U}(:, 1 : L), \tag{5}
$$

where $\mathbf{\Sigma}$ denotes the matrix whose diagonal elements are the singular values of $\mathbf{Y}_{(3)}$. $\mathbf{U}$ and $\mathbf{V}$ are the left and right singular matrices, respectively.

Equations (4) utilized the spectral correlation of HSI to reduce the dimensionality of the problem. Next, we explore the spatial correlation of coefficient tensor $\mathcal{L}$ to further enhance the model's performance. Specifically, we adopt the tensor nuclear norm (TNN) to characterize the low-rankness of coefficient tensor.

Moreover, it is recognized that disparities in imaging satellites, illumination conditions, and acquisition times can engender significant spectral variations between images [35], i.e., $\mathcal{Y}$ and $\mathcal{Z}$ come from different HR-HSIs. Thus, we incorporate a linear transformation to the spectral dimension of $\mathcal{Z}$. Finally, the RAF model is developed as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\min_{\mathcal{L},\tau,\mathbf{A},\mathcal{B}} & \|\mathcal{L}\|_{\text{TNN}}, \\
\text{s.t.} & \mathcal{H}_{\text{spa}}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) = \mathcal{Y} \circ \tau, \\
& \mathcal{H}_{\text{spec}}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) = \mathcal{Z} \times_3 \mathbf{A} + \mathcal{B},
\end{array}
\tag{6}
$$

where $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times h}$ and $\mathcal{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N \times h}$ are utilized to eradicate spectral discrepancies between images.

4.1.2 GGN algorithm for solving the RAF model

As a matter of fact, the equality constraint of (6) is highly nonlinear due to the domain transformations $\tau$, which complicates the minimization task. Therefore, we employ the Generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) algorithm, which involves leveraging a first-order approximation of $\tau$ when the variations in $\tau$ are relatively insignificant [19]. Specifically, under small perturbation $\Delta\tau$, we have $\mathcal{Y} \circ (\tau + \Delta\tau) \approx \mathcal{Y} \circ \tau + \mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau)$, with $\mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau) := \text{fold}_3((\sum_{i=1}^H \mathbf{J}_i \Delta\tau \epsilon_i \epsilon_i^\top)^\top)$, where $\mathbf{J}_i = \frac{\partial}{\partial \xi} \text{vec}(\mathcal{Y}_i \circ \xi)|_{\xi=\tau_i}$ is the Jacobian matrix of the $i$th image with respect to the transformation parameters $\tau_i$ and $\{\epsilon_i\}$ denotes the standard basis for $\mathbb{R}^H$. After adopting a local first-order approximation for a given $\tau^k$, we obtain the following subproblem:

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\min_{\mathcal{L}, \Delta\tau, \mathbf{A}, \mathcal{B}} & \|\mathcal{L}\|_{\text{TNN}}, \\
\text{s.t.} & \mathcal{H}_{\text{spa}}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) = \mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^k + \mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau), \\
& \mathcal{H}_{\text{spec}}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) = \mathcal{Z} \times_3 \mathbf{A} + \mathcal{B}.
\end{array}
\tag{7}
$$

Considering that subproblem (7) constitutes a local linearization of RAF model at the point $\tau^k$, we proceed to treat $\tau^k + \Delta\tau$ as the next iterative estimate and undertake another cycle of linearization. The entire procedure described above is summarized in Algorithm 1.

For the termination criterion of the algorithm, we define

$$
\kappa_{raf} := \frac{\|\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^{k+1}) - \mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{Z} \times_3 \mathbf{A}^{k+1} + \mathcal{B}^{k+1})\|}{\|\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{Z})\|}.
$$

The algorithm terminates when $\kappa_{raf}$ falls below a predetermined threshold. Next, we delve into the convergence properties associated with Algorithm 1.

minL,∆τ,A,B ∥L∥TNN, s.t. Hspa(L ×3 D) = Y ◦ τk + J(∆τ), (7) Hspec(L ×3 D) = Z ×3 A + B.

### 4.1.1 The RAF model

Given that HSIs typically encompass numerous spectral bands with high spectral correlation, we leverage subspace representation for \(\mathcal{X}\), i.e.,

\[
\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{L}\times_3\mathbf{D},
\tag{4}
\]

where \(\mathcal{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N\times L}\) is the coefficient tensor, \(\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times L}\) denotes dictionary and \(L\) represents the dimension of the subspace spanned by the columns of \(\mathbf{D}\). To estimate dictionary \(\mathbf{D}\), a commonly adopted assumption is that \(\mathcal{Y}\) and \(\mathcal{X}\) share a common spectral subspace. Employing this principle, we estimate the dictionary \(\mathbf{D}\) from the LR-HSI by applying truncated singular value decomposition (svd), i.e.,

\[
[\mathbf{U},\boldsymbol{\Sigma},\mathbf{V}]=\operatorname{svd}(\mathbf{Y}_{(3)})\quad \text{and}\quad \mathbf{D}=\mathbf{U}(:,1:L),
\tag{5}
\]

where \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) denotes the matrix whose diagonal elements are the singular values of \(\mathbf{Y}_{(3)}\). \(\mathbf{U}\) and \(\mathbf{V}\) are the left and right singular matrices, respectively.

Equations (4) utilized the spectral correlation of HSI to reduce the dimensionality of the problem. Next, we explore the spatial correlation of coefficient tensor \(\mathcal{L}\) to further enhance the model’s performance. Specifically, we adopt the tensor nuclear norm (TNN) to characterize the low-rankness of coefficient tensor.

Moreover, it is recognized that disparities in imaging satellites, illumination conditions, and acquisition times can engender significant spectral variations between images [35], i.e., \(\mathcal{Y}\) and \(\mathcal{Z}\) come from different HR-HSIs. Thus, we incorporate a linear transformation to the spectral dimension of \(\mathcal{Z}\). Finally, the RAF model is developed as follows:

\[
\min_{\mathcal{L},\tau,\mathbf{A},\mathcal{B}} \|\mathcal{L}\|_{\mathrm{TNN}},
\]

\[
s.t.\quad \mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L}\times_3\mathbf{D})=\mathcal{Y}\circ\tau,
\]

\[
\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L}\times_3\mathbf{D})=\mathcal{Z}\times_3\mathbf{A}+\mathcal{B},
\tag{6}
\]

where \(\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times h}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N\times h}\) are utilized to eradicate spectral discrepancies between images.

### 4.1.2 GGN algorithm for solving the RAF model

As a matter of fact, the equality constraint of (6) is highly nonlinear due to the domain transformations \(\tau\), which complicates the minimization task. Therefore, we employ the Generalized Gauss–Newton (GGN) algorithm, which involves leveraging a first-order approximation of \(\tau\) when the variations in \(\tau\) are relatively insignificant [19]. Specifically, under small perturbation \(\Delta\tau\), we have \(\mathcal{Y}\circ(\tau+\Delta\tau)\approx\mathcal{Y}\circ\tau+\mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau)\), with \(\mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau):=fold_3((\sum_{i=1}^{H}\mathbf{J}_i\Delta\tau_i\epsilon_i^{\top})^{\top})\),

where

\[
\mathbf{J}_i=\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\operatorname{vec}(\mathcal{Y}_i\circ\xi)\right|_{\xi=\tau_i}
\]

is the Jacobian matrix of the \(i\)th image with respect to the transformation parameters \(\tau_i\)

and \(\{\epsilon_i\}\) denotes the standard basis for \(\mathbb{R}^{H}\). After adopting a local first-order approximation for a given \(\tau^k\), we obtain the following subproblem:

\[
\min_{\mathcal{L},\Delta\tau,\mathbf{A},\mathcal{B}} \|\mathcal{L}\|_{\mathrm{TNN}},
\]

\[
s.t.\quad \mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L}\times_3\mathbf{D})=\mathcal{Y}\circ\tau^k+\mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau),
\]

\[
\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L}\times_3\mathbf{D})=\mathcal{Z}\times_3\mathbf{A}+\mathcal{B}.
\tag{7}
\]

Considering that subproblem (7) constitutes a local linearization of RAF model at the point \(\tau^k\), we proceed to treat \(\tau^k+\Delta\tau\) as the next iterative estimate and undertake another cycle of linearization. The entire procedure described above is summarized in Algorithm 1.

For the termination criterion of the algorithm, we define

\[
\kappa_{raf}:=
\frac{
\left\|\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{Y}\circ\tau^{k+1})-\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{Z}\times_3\mathbf{A}^{k+1}+\mathcal{B}^{k+1})\right\|
}{
\left\|\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{Z})\right\|
}.
\]

The algorithm terminates when \(\kappa_{raf}\) falls below a predetermined threshold. Next, we delve into the convergence properties associated with Algorithm 1.

**Theorem 4.1.** *Suppose the operator \(\mathcal{H}_{spa}\) satisfies \(REC(s)\) on set \(\mathbb{X}_s:=\{\mathcal{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N\times H}\mid rank(\mathcal{X}_{(3)})\leq s\}\), where \(s\) denotes the dimension of the null space of \(\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\cdot)\), then Algorithm 1 converges quadratically in the neighborhood of any strongly unique local minimum of (6).*

The proof is provided in the Appendix B.

**Remark 4.1.** *Within the framework of the RAF model, the obtained \(\mathcal{X}\) can be decomposed into \(\mathcal{L}\times_3\mathbf{D}\), which indicates that \(rank(\mathcal{X}_{(3)})\leq rank(\mathcal{L}_{(3)})\leq L\). Consequently, \(L\) serves as an upper threshold on the value of \(s\), inherently suggesting that \(s\) is constrained from becoming excessively large.*

Specifically, under small perturbation \(\Delta \tau\), we have \(\mathcal{Y} \circ (\tau + \Delta \tau) \approx \mathcal{Y} \circ \tau + \mathcal{J}(\Delta \tau)\), with \(\mathcal{J}(\Delta \tau) := fold_3((\sum_{i=1}^H \mathbf{J}_i \Delta \tau_i \epsilon_i^\top)^\top)\), where \(\mathbf{J}_i = \frac{\partial}{\partial \xi} \text{vec}(\mathcal{Y}_i \circ \xi)|_{\xi=\tau_i}\) is the Jacobian matrix of the \(i\)th image with respect to the transformation parameters \(\tau_i\) and \(\{\epsilon_i\}\) denotes the standard basis for \(\mathbb{R}^H\). After adopting a local first-order approximation for a given \(\tau^k\), we obtain the following subproblem: \[ \min_{\mathcal{L}, \Delta \tau, \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}} \|\mathcal{L}\|_{\text{TNN}}, \quad s.t. \quad \mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) = \mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^k + \mathcal{J}(\Delta \tau), \quad \mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) = \mathcal{Z} \times_3 \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}. \] Considering that subproblem (7) constitutes a local linearization of RAF model at the point \(\tau^k\), we proceed to treat \(\tau^k + \Delta \tau\) as the next iterative estimate and undertake another cycle of linearization. The entire procedure described above is summarized in Algorithm 1. For the termination criterion of the algorithm, we define \[ \kappa_{raf} := \frac{\|\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^{k+1}) - \mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{Z} \times_3 \mathbf{A}^{k+1} + \mathbf{B}^{k+1})\|}{\|\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{Z})\|}. \] The algorithm terminates when \(\kappa_{raf}\) falls below a predetermined threshold. Next, we delve into the convergence properties associated with Algorithm 1. **Theorem 4.1.** _Suppose the operator \(\mathcal{H}_{spa}\) satisfies \(REC(s)\) on set \(\mathbb{X}_s := \{\mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N \times H} \mid rank(\mathcal{X}_{(3)}) \leq s\}\), where \(s\) denotes the dimension of the null space of \(\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\cdot)\), then Algorithm 1 converges quadratically in the neighborhood of any strongly unique local minimum of (6)._ The proof is provided in the Appendix B. **Remark 4.1.** _Within the framework of the RAF model, the obtained \(\mathcal{X}\) can be decomposed into \(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}\), which indicates that \(rank(\mathcal{X}_{(3)}) \leq rank(\mathcal{L}_{(3)}) \leq L\). Consequently, \(L\) serves as an upper threshold on the value of \(s\), inherently suggesting that \(s\) is constrained from becoming excessively large._

Although model (7) is convex, the direct utilization of ADMM for solving it may fail to converge given that the number of variables surpasses two [45]. Firstly, by denoting \tilde{\mathcal{Z}} := \mathcal{Z} \times_3 \mathbf{A} + \mathcal{B}, the augmented Lagrangian function of (7) is defined as

\begin{aligned} \Theta(\mathcal{L}, \Delta\tau, \mathbf{A}, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{O}_1, \mathcal{O}_2) := & \frac{\mu_1}{2} \|\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - (\mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^k + \mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau)) + \frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1}\|_F^2 \\ & + \frac{\mu_2}{2} \|\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - \tilde{\mathcal{Z}} + \frac{\mathcal{O}_2}{\mu_2}\|_F^2 + \|\mathcal{L}\|_{\text{TNN}}, \end{aligned} \quad (8)

where the symbols \mathcal{O}_1 and \mathcal{O}_2 represent Lagrangian multipliers. \mu_1 and \mu_2 are two positive penalty parameters. The iterative scheme of sGS-ADMM is given explicitly by

\begin{aligned} \Delta\tau^{t+\frac{1}{2}} &= \arg \min_{\Delta\tau} \{\Theta(\mathcal{L}^t, \Delta\tau, \mathbf{A}^t, \mathcal{B}^t, \mathcal{O}_1^t, \mathcal{O}_2^t)\}, \\ \mathcal{L}^{t+1} &= \arg \min_{\mathcal{L}} \{\Theta(\mathcal{L}, \Delta\tau^{t+\frac{1}{2}}, \mathbf{A}^t, \mathcal{B}^t, \mathcal{O}_1^t, \mathcal{O}_2^t)\}, \\ \Delta\tau^{t+1} &= \arg \min_{\Delta\tau} \{\Theta(\mathcal{L}^{t+1}, \Delta\tau, \mathbf{A}^t, \mathcal{B}^t, \mathcal{O}_1^t, \mathcal{O}_2^t)\}, \\ (\mathbf{A}^{t+1}, \mathcal{B}^{t+1}) &= \arg \min_{\mathbf{A}, \mathcal{B}} \{\Theta(\mathcal{L}^{t+1}, \Delta\tau^{t+1}, \mathbf{A}, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{O}_1^t, \mathcal{O}_2^t)\}, \\ \mathcal{O}_1^{t+1} &= \mathcal{O}_1^t + \rho\mu_1(\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L}^{t+1} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - (\mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^k + \mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau^{t+1}))), \\ \mathcal{O}_2^{t+1} &= \mathcal{O}_2^t + \rho\mu_2(\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L}^{t+1} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - \tilde{\mathcal{Z}}^{t+1}), \end{aligned} \quad (9)

where \rho \in (0, (1 + \sqrt{5})/2) is the step length. Subsequently, we proceed to solve each of the subproblems.

a. The subproblem \Delta\tau is
\min_{\Delta\tau} \|\mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau) + \mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^k - \mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - \frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1}\|_F^2. \quad (10)
The optimal solution of (10) can be given by
\Delta\tau = \sum_{i=1}^H \mathbf{J}_i^\dagger \mathbf{M} \varepsilon_i^\top, \quad (11)

where \mathbf{M} := (\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) + \frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1} - \mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^k)_{(3)}^\top and \mathbf{J}_i^\dagger denotes the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of \mathbf{J}_i.

b. The subproblem \mathcal{L} is
\min_{\mathcal{L}} \frac{\mu_1}{2} \|\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - (\mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^k + \mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau)) + \frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1}\|_F^2 + \frac{\mu_2}{2} \|\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - \tilde{\mathcal{Z}} + \frac{\mathcal{O}_2}{\mu_2}\|_F^2 + \|\mathcal{L}\|_{\text{TNN}}. \quad (12)
By introducing the variable \mathcal{G} = \mathcal{L}, (12) is reformulated as
\begin{aligned} \min_{\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{G}} & \frac{\mu_1}{2} \|\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - (\mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^k + \mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau)) + \frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1}\|_F^2 + \frac{\mu_2}{2} \|\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - \tilde{\mathcal{Z}} + \frac{\mathcal{O}_2}{\mu_2}\|_F^2 + \|\mathcal{G}\|_{\text{TNN}}, \\ \text{s.t.} & \quad \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{G}. \end{aligned}

Although model (7) is convex, the direct utilization of ADMM for solving it may fail to converge given that the number of variables surpasses two [45]. Therefore, we employ the symmetric Gauss–Seidel ADMM [46, 47]. Firstly, by denoting 𝒵̄ := 𝒵 ×₃ 𝐀 + ℬ, the augmented Lagrangian function of (7) is defined as

## 4.1.3 sGS-ADMM for solving model (7)

Although model (7) is convex, the direct utilization of ADMM for solving it may fail to converge given that the number of variables surpasses two [45]. Therefore, we employ the symmetric Gauss-Seidel ADMM [46, 47]. Firstly, by denoting \(\bar{\mathcal{Z}} := \mathcal{Z} \times_3 \mathbf{A} + \mathcal{B}\), the augmented Lagrangian function of (7) is defined as

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Theta(\mathcal{L}, \Delta\tau, \mathbf{A}, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{O}_1, \mathcal{O}_2) :=&
\frac{\mu_1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L}\times_3\mathbf{D})-(\mathcal{Y}\circ\tau^k+\mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau))+\frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1}\right\|_F^2 \\
&+\frac{\mu_2}{2}\left\|\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L}\times_3\mathbf{D})-\bar{\mathcal{Z}}+\frac{\mathcal{O}_2}{\mu_2}\right\|_F^2+\|\mathcal{L}\|_{\mathrm{TNN}},
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]

where the symbols \(\mathcal{O}_1\) and \(\mathcal{O}_2\) represent Lagrangian multipliers. \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) are two positive penalty parameters. The iterative scheme of sGS-ADMM is given explicitly by

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta\tau^{t+\frac{1}{2}} &= \arg\min_{\Delta\tau}\{\Theta(\mathcal{L}^t,\Delta\tau,\mathbf{A}^t,\mathcal{B}^t,\mathcal{O}_1^t,\mathcal{O}_2^t)\},\\
\mathcal{L}^{t+1} &= \arg\min_{\mathcal{L}}\{\Theta(\mathcal{L},\Delta\tau^{t+\frac{1}{2}},\mathbf{A}^t,\mathcal{B}^t,\mathcal{O}_1^t,\mathcal{O}_2^t)\},\\
\Delta\tau^{t+1} &= \arg\min_{\Delta\tau}\{\Theta(\mathcal{L}^{t+1},\Delta\tau,\mathbf{A}^t,\mathcal{B}^t,\mathcal{O}_1^t,\mathcal{O}_2^t)\},\\
(\mathbf{A}^{t+1},\mathcal{B}^{t+1}) &= \arg\min_{\mathbf{A},\mathcal{B}}\{\Theta(\mathcal{L}^{t+1},\Delta\tau^{t+1},\mathbf{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{O}_1^t,\mathcal{O}_2^t)\},\\
\mathcal{O}_1^{t+1} &= \mathcal{O}_1^t+\rho\mu_1(\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L}^{t+1}\times_3\mathbf{D})-(\mathcal{Y}\circ\tau^k+\mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau^{t+1}))),\\
\mathcal{O}_2^{t+1} &= \mathcal{O}_2^t+\rho\mu_2(\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L}^{t+1}\times_3\mathbf{D})-\bar{\mathcal{Z}}^{t+1}),
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]

where \(\rho \in (0,(1+\sqrt{5})/2)\) is the step length. Subsequently, we proceed to solve each of the subproblems.

**a.** The subproblem \(\Delta\tau\) is

\[
\min_{\Delta\tau}\left\|\mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau)+\mathcal{Y}\circ\tau^k-\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L}\times_3\mathbf{D})-\frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1}\right\|_F^2.
\tag{10}
\]

The optimal solution of (10) can be given by

\[
\Delta\tau=\sum_{i=1}^{H}\mathbf{J}_i^{\dagger}\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i^{\top},
\tag{11}
\]

where \(\mathbf{M}:=(\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L}\times_3\mathbf{D})+\frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1}-\mathcal{Y}\circ\tau^k)_{(3)}^{\top}\) and \(\mathbf{J}_i^{\dagger}\) denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of \(\mathbf{J}_i\).

**b.** The subproblem \(\mathcal{L}\) is

\[
\min_{\mathcal{L}}\frac{\mu_1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L}\times_3\mathbf{D})-(\mathcal{Y}\circ\tau^k+\mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau))+\frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1}\right\|_F^2
+\frac{\mu_2}{2}\left\|\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L}\times_3\mathbf{D})-\bar{\mathcal{Z}}+\frac{\mathcal{O}_2}{\mu_2}\right\|_F^2+\|\mathcal{L}\|_{\mathrm{TNN}}.
\tag{12}
\]

By introducing the variable \(\mathcal{G}=\mathcal{L}\), (12) is reformulated as

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\mathcal{L},\mathcal{G}}\quad &
\frac{\mu_1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L}\times_3\mathbf{D})-(\mathcal{Y}\circ\tau^k+\mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau))+\frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1}\right\|_F^2 \\
&+\frac{\mu_2}{2}\left\|\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L}\times_3\mathbf{D})-\bar{\mathcal{Z}}+\frac{\mathcal{O}_2}{\mu_2}\right\|_F^2+\|\mathcal{G}\|_{\mathrm{TNN}},\\
\text{s.t.}\quad & \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{G}.
\end{aligned}
\]

J_i^k=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\mathrm{vec}\left(Y(:, :, i)\circ x\right)\right)\Bigg|_{x=\tau_i^k},\quad i=1,\ldots,H;
\]

2: Compute \((L^{k+1}, \Delta\tau^{k+1}, A^{k+1}, B^{k+1})\) by solving (7);  
3: Update \(\tau^{k+1}=\tau^k+\Delta\tau^{k+1}\);  
4: If converge, algorithm terminates;  
else, set \(k=k+1\) and goto step1;

**Output:** \(L^{k+1}, \tau^{k+1}, A^{k+1}, B^{k+1}\).

## 4.1.3 sGS-ADMM for solving model (7)

Although model (7) is convex, the direct utilization of ADMM for solving it may fail to converge given that the number of variables surpasses two [45]. Therefore, we employ the symmetric Gauss–Seidel ADMM [46, 47]. Firstly, by denoting \(\bar{z} := Z \leftrightarrow Z \leftrightarrow A + B\), the augmented Lagrangian function of (7) is defined as

\[
\Theta(L,\Delta\tau,A,B,O_1,O_2)
=\frac{\mu_1}{2}\left\|H_{spa}(L\times 3D)-(Y\circ \tau^k+J(\Delta\tau))\right\|_F^2
+\frac{\mu_2}{2}\left\|H_{spec}(L\times 3D)-\bar{Z}\right\|_F^2
+\frac{O_1}{\mu_1}\|F
+\frac{O_2}{\mu_2}\|F
+\|L\|_{TNN},
\tag{8}
\]

where the symbols \(O_1\) and \(O_2\) represent Lagrangian multipliers. \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) are two positive penalty parameters. The iterative scheme of sGS-ADMM is given by

\[
\Delta\tau^{t+\frac{1}{2}}
=\arg\min_{\Delta\tau}\Theta(L^t,\Delta\tau,A^t,B^t,O_1^t,O_2^t),
\tag{9}
\]

\[
L^{t+1}
=\arg\min_{L}\Theta(L,\Delta\tau^{t+\frac{1}{2}},A^t,B^t,O_1^t,O_2^t),
\tag{9}
\]

\[
\Delta\tau^{t+1}
=\arg\min_{\Delta\tau}\Theta(L^{t+1},\Delta\tau,A^t,B^t,O_1^t,O_2^t),
\tag{9}
\]

\[
(A^{t+1},B^{t+1})
=\arg\min_{A,B}\Theta(L^{t+1},\Delta\tau^{t+1},A,B,O_1^t,O_2^t),
\tag{9}
\]

\[
O_1^{t+1}
=O_1^t+\rho\mu_1\left(H_{spa}(L^{t+1}\times 3D)-(Y\circ \tau^{t+1}+J(\Delta\tau^{t+1}))\right),
\]

\[
O_2^{t+1}
=O_2^t+\rho\mu_2\left(H_{spec}(L^{t+1}\times 3D)-\bar{Z}^{t+1}\right),
\]

where \(\rho\in(0,(1+\sqrt{5})/2)\) is the step length. Subsequently, we proceed to solve each of the subproblems.

### a. The subproblem \(\Delta\tau\) is

\[
\min_{\Delta\tau}\ \left\|J(\Delta\tau)+Y\circ \tau^k-H_{spa}(L\times 3D)\right\|_F^2
-\frac{O_1}{\mu_1}\|F,
\tag{10}
\]

The optimal solution of (10) can be given by

\[
\Delta\tau=\sum_{i=1}^{H}J_i^{\dagger}M_i\epsilon_i^T,
\tag{11}
\]

where \(M=(H_{spa}(L\times 3D)+\frac{O_1}{\mu_1}-Y\circ \tau^k)^T\) and \(J_i^{\dagger}\) denotes the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of \(J_i\).

### b. The subproblem \(L\) is

\[
\min_{L}\ \frac{\mu_1}{2}\left\|H_{spa}(L\times 3D)-(Y\circ \tau^k+J(\Delta\tau))+\frac{O_1}{\mu_1}\right\|_F^2
+\frac{\mu_2}{2}\left\|H_{spec}(L\times 3D)-\bar{Z}+\frac{O_2}{\mu_2}\right\|_F^2
+\|L\|_{TNN}.
\tag{12}
\]

By introducing the variable \(G=L\), (12) is reformulated as

\[
\min_{L,G}\ \frac{\mu_1}{1}\left\|H_{spa}(L\times 3D)-(Y\circ \tau^k+J(\Delta\tau))+\frac{O_1}{\mu_1}\right\|_F
+\frac{\mu_2}{2}\left\|H_{spec}(L\times 3D)-\bar{Z}+\frac{O_2}{\mu_2}\right\|_F
+\|G\|_{TNN},
\]

**s.t.** \(L=G\).

**Input:** 𝒴, 𝒵, **D**.  
**Initialize:** 𝓛⁰, τ⁰, **A**⁰, **B**⁰. Set k = 0.

\]

3: Update \(\tau^{k+1} = \tau^k + \Delta \tau^{k+1}\);  
4: If converge, algorithm terminates;  
else, set \(k = k + 1\) and goto step1;  
**Output:** \(\mathcal{L}^{k+1}, \tau^{k+1}, \mathbf{A}^{k+1}, \mathbf{B}^{k+1}\).

### 4.1.3 sGS-ADMM for solving model (7)

Although model (7) is convex, the direct utilization of ADMM for solving it may fail to converge given that the number of variables surpasses two [45]. Therefore, we employ the symmetric Gauss–Seidel ADMM [46, 47]. Firstly, by denoting \(\bar{\mathcal{Z}} := \mathcal{Z} \times_3 \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}\), the augmented Lagrangian function of (7) is defined as

\[
\Theta(\mathcal{L}, \Delta \tau, \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}, \mathcal{O}_1, \mathcal{O}_2) := \frac{\mu_1}{2} \|\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - (\mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^k + \mathcal{J}(\Delta \tau)) + \frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1}\|_F^2
\]
\[
+ \frac{\mu_2}{2} \|\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - \bar{\mathcal{Z}} + \frac{\mathcal{O}_2}{\mu_2}\|_F^2 + \|\mathcal{L}\|_{TNN},
\]
(8)

where the symbols \(\mathcal{O}_1\) and \(\mathcal{O}_2\) represent Lagrangian multipliers. \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) are two positive penalty parameters. The iterative scheme of sGS-ADMM is given explicitly by

\[
\Delta \tau^{t+\frac{1}{2}} = \arg \min_{\Delta \tau} \{\Theta(\mathcal{L}^t, \Delta \tau, \mathbf{A}^t, \mathbf{B}^t, \mathcal{O}_1^t, \mathcal{O}_2^t)\},
\]
\[
\mathcal{L}^{t+1} = \arg \min_{\mathcal{L}} \{\Theta(\mathcal{L}, \Delta \tau^{t+\frac{1}{2}}, \mathbf{A}^t, \mathbf{B}^t, \mathcal{O}_1^t, \mathcal{O}_2^t)\},
\]
\[
\Delta \tau^{t+1} = \arg \min_{\Delta \tau} \{\Theta(\mathcal{L}^{t+1}, \Delta \tau, \mathbf{A}^t, \mathbf{B}^t, \mathcal{O}_1^t, \mathcal{O}_2^t)\},
\]
\[
(\mathbf{A}^{t+1}, \mathbf{B}^{t+1}) = \arg \min_{\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}} \{\Theta(\mathcal{L}^{t+1}, \Delta \tau^{t+1}, \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}, \mathcal{O}_1^t, \mathcal{O}_2^t)\},
\]
\[
\mathcal{O}_1^{t+1} = \mathcal{O}_1^t + \rho \mu_1 (\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L}^{t+1} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - (\mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^k + \mathcal{J}(\Delta \tau^{t+1}))),
\]
\[
\mathcal{O}_2^{t+1} = \mathcal{O}_2^t + \rho \mu_2 (\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L}^{t+1} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - \bar{\mathcal{Z}}^{t+1}),
\]
(9)

where \(\rho \in (0, (1 + \sqrt{5})/2)\) is the step length. Subsequently, we proceed to solve each of the subproblems.

**a.** The subproblem \(\Delta \tau\) is

\[
\min_{\Delta \tau} \|\mathcal{J}(\Delta \tau) + \mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^k - \mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - \frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1}\|_F^2.
\]
(10)

The optimal solution of (10) can be given by

\[
\Delta \tau = \sum_{i=1}^H \mathbf{J}_i^\dagger \mathbf{M}_{i} \varepsilon_i^\top,
\]
(11)

where \(\mathbf{M} := (\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) + \frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1} - \mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^k)_{(3)}^\top\) and \(\mathbf{J}_i^\dagger\) denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of \(\mathbf{J}_i\).

**b.** The subproblem \(\mathcal{L}\) is

\[
\min_{\mathcal{L}} \frac{\mu_1}{2} \|\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - (\mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^k + \mathcal{J}(\Delta \tau)) + \frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1}\|_F^2 + \frac{\mu_2}{2} \|\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - \bar{\mathcal{Z}} + \frac{\mathcal{O}_2}{\mu_2}\|_F^2 + \|\mathcal{L}\|_{TNN}.
\]
(12)

By introducing the variable \(\mathcal{G} = \mathcal{L}\), (12) is reformulated as

\[
\min_{\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{G}} \frac{\mu_1}{2} \|\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - (\mathcal{Y} \circ \tau^k + \mathcal{J}(\Delta \tau)) + \frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1}\|_F^2 + \frac{\mu_2}{2} \|\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - \bar{\mathcal{Z}} + \frac{\mathcal{O}_2}{\mu_2}\|_F^2 + \|\mathcal{G}\|_{TNN},
\]
\[
s.t. \quad \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{G}.
\]

The augmented Lagrangian function is

\begin{aligned} \min_{\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{G}, \mathcal{O}} \quad & \frac{\mu_1}{2} \|\mathcal{H}_{spa}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - (\mathcal{V} \circ \tau^k + \mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau)) + \frac{\mathcal{O}_1}{\mu_1} \|_F^2 + \frac{\mu_2}{2} \|\mathcal{H}_{spec}(\mathcal{L} \times_3 \mathbf{D}) - \tilde{\mathcal{Z}} + \frac{\mathcal{O}_2}{\mu_2} \|_F^2 + \|\mathcal{G}\|_{\text{TNN}}, \\ & + \frac{\nu}{2} \|\mathcal{L} - \mathcal{G} - \frac{\mathcal{O}}{\nu} \|_F^2. \end{aligned}

The variable \mathcal{L} can be updated by solving the optimality condition with respect to \mathcal{L}, which is a Sylvester equation:

\mathbf{H}_1 \mathcal{L}_{(3)} + \mathcal{L}_{(3)} \mathbf{H}_2 = \mathbf{H}_3. \quad (13)

Given that \mathbf{D}^\top \mathbf{D} = \mathbf{I}, we can denote

\begin{aligned} \mathbf{H}_1 &:= \mu_2 (\mathbf{R}\mathbf{D})^\top \mathbf{R}\mathbf{D} + \nu \mathbf{I}_L, \\ \mathbf{H}_2 &:= \mu_1 \mathbf{B}\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{S})^\top, \\ \mathbf{H}_3 &:= \mu_1 \mathbf{P}(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{S})^\top + \mu_2 (\mathbf{R}\mathbf{D})^\top \mathbf{Q} + (\nu \mathcal{G} - \mathcal{O})_{(3)}, \end{aligned} \quad (14)

where

\begin{aligned} \mathbf{P} &= (\mathcal{V} \circ \tau^k + \mathcal{J}(\Delta\tau) - \mathcal{O}_1/\mu_1)_{(3)}, \\ \mathbf{Q} &= (\tilde{\mathcal{Z}} - \mathcal{O}_2/\mu_2)_{(3)}. \end{aligned}

Equation (13) has a closed-form solution which can be solved efficiently by Algorithm 2.

Algorithm 2 A closed-form solution of (13)

Input: \mathbf{H}_1, \mathbf{H}_2, \mathbf{H}_3, \mathbf{B}, \mathbf{S}.

  1. 1: Eigen-decomposition of \mathbf{B} : \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{F}\mathbf{K}\mathbf{F}^H;
  2. 2: \tilde{\mathbf{K}} = \mathbf{K}(\mathbf{I}_d \otimes \mathbf{1}_{mn});
  3. 3: Eigen-decomposition of \mathbf{H}_1 : \mathbf{H}_1 = \mathbf{Q}_1 \Lambda \mathbf{Q}_1^H;
  4. 4: \tilde{\mathbf{H}}_3 = \mathbf{Q}_1^{-1} \mathbf{H}_3 \mathbf{F};
  5. 5: for i = 1 : L do
  6. 6: \tilde{\mathbf{L}}(i, :) = \lambda_i^{-1} (\tilde{\mathbf{H}}_3)_i - \lambda_i^{-1} (\tilde{\mathbf{H}}_3)_i \tilde{\mathbf{K}}(\lambda_i d \mathbf{I}_n + \sum_{t=1}^d \mathbf{K}_t^2) \tilde{\mathbf{K}}^H;
  7. 7: end for
  8. 8: Set \mathbf{L} = \mathbf{Q}_1 \tilde{\mathbf{L}} \mathbf{F}^H;

Output: \mathcal{L} = \text{fold}_3(\mathbf{L}).

In this algorithm, \lambda_i, i = 1, \dots, L are the diagonal elements of \Lambda and d is the spatial degradation factor. Further particulars of the algorithm can be located in reference [48].

The \mathcal{G} subproblem is

\mathcal{G}^{t+1} \in \arg \min_{\mathcal{G}} \|\mathcal{G}\|_{\text{TNN}} + \frac{\nu}{2} \|\mathcal{G} - \mathcal{L} - \frac{\mathcal{O}}{\nu} \|_F^2. \quad (15)

Capitalizing on tensor Singular Value Thresholding (t-SVT, [37]), model (15) admits a closed-form solution, that is

\mathcal{G}^{t+1} = \mathcal{U} * \mathcal{D} * \mathcal{V}^H, \quad (16)

where \mathcal{U} * \mathcal{S} * \mathcal{V}^H represents the t-SVD of (\mathcal{L} + \mathcal{O}/\nu). \mathcal{D} and \mathcal{S} are f-diagonal tensors with \mathcal{D} = \text{ift}(\max\{\hat{\mathcal{S}} - \frac{1}{\nu}, 0\}, [ ], 3), where \hat{\mathcal{S}} := \text{fft}(\mathcal{S}, [ ], 3). Lastly, the iterative update for the Lagrangian multiplier \mathcal{O} can be given by

Considering that the RAF model performs multiple tasks simultaneously, it may not consistently yield the optimal fusion outcome. Therefore, in this section, we propose the novel NLRGS model, specifically designed to enhance the fusion performance and robustness.

4.2.1 The NLRGS model

Presently, the majority of fusion algorithms primarily focus on designing strategies to reconstruct the principal image content with superior quality. Nevertheless, they frequently fail to capitalize on the potential of extracting additional information from the residual components within the images. This oversight may lead to an inefficient use of the available image data, and a missed opportunity for enhancing the overall fusion performance. Consequently, we propose to partition the target \mathcal{X} into two distinct components: a primary component, \tilde{\mathcal{L}}, and a residual component, \tilde{\mathcal{E}}, such that \mathcal{X} can be expressed as \mathcal{X} = \tilde{\mathcal{L}} + \tilde{\mathcal{E}}. The core objective is to reconstruct both \tilde{\mathcal{L}} and \tilde{\mathcal{E}} by thoroughly exploring and leveraging their unique characteristics and information content.

With respect to the primary component \tilde{\mathcal{L}}, we adopt the subspace representation approach as utilized in (4). In terms of dictionary selection, we employ the same approach:

[\mathbf{U}, \Sigma, \mathbf{V}] = \text{svd}(\mathbf{Y}_R) \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{D}_{\mathcal{L}} = \mathbf{U}(:, 1 : L_1), \quad (19)

where \mathbf{Y}_R := \text{unfold}_3(\mathcal{Y}_R) and \mathcal{Y}_R represents the registered HSI obtained from RAF model. Observing that the coefficient tensor under dictionary \mathbf{D}_{\mathcal{L}} retains a comprehensive spatial structure, we incorporate the nonlocal self-similarity inherent in images, which clusters similar patches together to form 4th-order tensors. This is designed to bolster the low-rank prior characteristic of the data.

Regarding the residual component \tilde{\mathcal{E}}, directly updating it can be computationally expensive due to its size being equivalent to that of the target \mathcal{X}. Therefore, we also project \tilde{\mathcal{E}} into a low-dimensional subspace along the spectral mode, i.e.,

\tilde{\mathcal{E}} = \mathcal{E} \times_3 \mathbf{D}_{\mathcal{E}}, \quad (20)

where \mathcal{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N \times L_2} represents the coefficient tensor, \mathbf{D}_{\mathcal{E}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times L_2} denotes the dictionary and L_2 is the dimension of the subspace spanned by the columns of \mathbf{D}_{\mathcal{E}}. This not only reduces the dimensionality of the problem but also enhances the robustness of the high-frequency information in \tilde{\mathcal{E}}. \mathbf{D}_{\mathcal{E}} = \mathbf{U}(:, L_1 + 1 : L_1 + L_2), \quad (21)

Algorithm 3 sGS-ADMM algorithm for solving (7)
Input: 𝒴, 𝒵, 𝜏𝑘, 𝜇1, 𝜇2, 𝜈, 𝜃.
Initialize: ℒ0, 𝒢0, Δ𝜏0, 𝐀0, ℬ0. Set 𝑡 = 0.
1: Compute Δ𝜏𝑡+½ by (11);
2: Compute ℒ𝑡+1 by solving (12);
3: Compute Δ𝜏𝑡+1 by (11);
4: Compute (𝐀𝑡+1, ℬ𝑡+1) by (18);
5: Update multipliers 𝒪1𝑡+1 and 𝒪2𝑡+1 as (9).
6: If converge, algorithm terminates;
else, set 𝑡 = 𝑡 + 1 and goto step1;
Output: ℒ𝑡+1, Δ𝜏𝑡+1, 𝐀𝑡+1 and ℬ𝑡+1.
Theorem 4.2. Suppose that 𝜌 ∈ (0, (1 + √5)/2). Let the sequence {ℒ𝑡, Δ𝜏𝑡, (𝐀𝑡, ℬ𝑡), 𝒪1𝑡, 𝒪2𝑡}𝑡∈ℕ be generated by Algorithm 3. Then the sequence {ℒ𝑡, Δ𝜏𝑡, (𝐀𝑡, ℬ𝑡)}𝑡∈ℕ converges to an optimal solution of (7) and the sequence {𝒪1𝑡, 𝒪2𝑡}𝑡∈ℕ converges to an optimal solution to the dual of (7).
4.2 The NLRGS model and algorithm
Considering that the RAF model performs multiple tasks simultaneously, it may not consistently yield the optimal fusion outcome. Therefore, in this section, we propose the novel NLRGS model, specifically designed to enhance the fusion performance and robustness.
4.2.1 The NLRGS model
Presently, the majority of fusion algorithms primarily focus on designing strategies to reconstruct the principal image content with superior quality. Nevertheless, they frequently fail to capitalize on the potential of extracting additional information from the residual components within the images. This oversight may lead to an inefficient use of the available image data, and a missed opportunity for enhancing the overall fusion performance. Consequently, we propose to partition the target 𝒳 into two distinct components: a primary component, ℒ̃, and a residual component, ℰ̃, such that 𝒳 can be expressed as 𝒳 = ℒ̃ + ℰ̃. The core objective is to reconstruct both ℒ̃ and ℰ̃ by thoroughly exploring and leveraging their unique characteristics and information content.
With respect to the primary component ℒ̃, we adopt the subspace representation approach as utilized in (4). In terms of dictionary selection, we employ the same approach:
[𝐔, Σ, 𝐕] = svd(𝐘𝑅) and 𝐃ℒ = 𝐔(:, 1 : 𝐿1), (19)
where 𝐘𝑅 := 𝑢𝑛𝑓𝑜𝑙𝑑3(𝒴𝑅) and 𝒴𝑅 represents the registered HSI obtained from RAF model. Observing that the coefficient tensor under dictionary 𝐃ℒ retains a comprehensive spatial structure, we incorporate the nonlocal self-similarity inherent in images, which clusters similar patches together to form 4th-order tensors. This is designed to bolster the low-rank prior characteristic of the data.
Regarding the residual component ℰ̃, directly updating it can be computationally expensive due to its size being equivalent to that of the target 𝒳. Therefore, we also project ℰ̃ into a low-dimensional subspace along the spectral mode, i.e.,
ℰ̃ = ℰ ×3 𝐃ℰ, (20)
where ℰ ∈ ℝ𝑀×𝑁×𝐿2 represents the coefficient tensor, 𝐃ℰ ∈ ℝ𝐻×𝐿2 denotes the dictionary and 𝐿2 is the dimension of the subspace spanned by the columns of 𝐃ℰ. This not only reduces the dimensionality of the problem but also enhances the robustness of the high-frequency information in ℰ̃. As for the estimation of 𝐃ℰ, we intuitively consider that the subspace generated by the column vectors of 𝐃ℰ should have no intersection with the subspace spanned by 𝐃ℒ associated with the primary component.
